Short proofs of the Quantum Substate Theorem

December 30, 2011
Abstract

The Quantum Substate Theorem due to Jain, Radhakrishnan, and Sen (2002) gives us a powerful operational interpretation of relative entropy, in fact, of the observational divergence of two quantum states, a quantity that is related to their relative entropy. Informally, the theorem states that if the observational divergence between two quantum states ρ,σ\rho,\sigma is small, then there is a quantum state ρ′\rho^{\prime} close to ρ\rho in trace distance, such that ρ′\rho^{\prime} when scaled down by a small factor becomes a substate of σ\sigma. We present new proofs of this theorem. The resulting statement is optimal up to a constant factor in its dependence on observational divergence. In addition, the proofs are both conceptually simpler and significantly shorter than the earlier proof.

1 The Quantum Substate Theorem

Consider quantum states ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}), where ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}} is a finite dimensional Hilbert space ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}, and D⁡(ℋ){{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) denotes the set of all quantum states with support in ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}, i.e., the set of unit trace positive semi-definite operators on ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}. We say that ρ\rho is a cc-substate of σ\sigma if ρ⪯2c​σ\rho\preceq 2^{c}\sigma, where ⪯\preceq represents the Löwner partial order on operators on ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}. We may equivalently express this condition in terms of measurement outcomes (“POVM elements”) as follows. Let

P⁡(ℋ)=𝖽𝖾𝖿{M∈L⁡(ℋ):O⪯M⪯I},{{\mathrm{P}}}({{\mathcal{H}}})\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\quad\left\{M\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}})\;:\;O\preceq M\preceq{{\mathrm{I}}}\right\}\kern 5.0pt,

denote the set of POVM elements on ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}, where L⁡(ℋ){{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) is the space of linear operators and I{{\mathrm{I}}} is the identity operator on ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}. The state ρ\rho is a cc-substate of σ\sigma iff for every measurement outcome M∈P⁡(ℋ)M\in{{\mathrm{P}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}), the probability Tr⁡(M​σ)\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(M\sigma) of observing MM when σ\sigma is measured according to the POVM {M,I−M}\left\{M,{{\mathrm{I}}}-M\right\} is at least Tr⁡(M​ρ)/2c\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(M\rho)/2^{c}, a 1/2c1/2^{c} fraction of the probability of observing MM when ρ\rho is measured. Morally, the state σ\sigma may be decomposed as σ=α​ρ+(1−α)​σ~\sigma=\alpha\rho+(1-\alpha)\tilde{\sigma}, for some σ~∈D⁡(ℋ)\tilde{\sigma}\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}), with α≥1/2c\alpha\geq 1/2^{c}. This in turn may be used to construct the state ρ\rho from σ\sigma through quantum analogues of rejection sampling. For example, we may apply the quantum measurement specified by the Kraus operators {αρ1/2σ−1/2,1−ασ~1/2σ−1/2}\left\{\sqrt{\alpha}\,\rho^{1/2}\sigma^{-1/2},\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,\tilde{\sigma}^{1/2}\sigma^{-1/2}\right\}, or go through a purification of σ\sigma [8, 10].

Given arbitrary quantum states ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) we are interested in how well σ\sigma masquerades as ρ\rho in the above sense. In other words, we are interested in the least cc such that ρ\rho is a cc-substate of σ\sigma. We call this quantity the relative min-entropy 𝖲∞(ρ∥σ){{\mathsf{S}}}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma) of the two states. A generalization of this notion to bipartite states has been studied by Renner [14, Chapter 3], and the notion itself has been studied by Datta [2] as “max-relative entropy”. For typical applications, such as privacy trade-offs in communication protocols [8, 10], it suffices to construct an approximation ρ′\rho^{\prime} to ρ\rho, with respect to a metric on quantum states. This leads us to the notion of the smooth relative min-entropy 𝖲∞ε(ρ∥σ){{\mathsf{S}}}^{\varepsilon}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma) of the two states, a quantity implicitly studied by Jain, Radhakrishnan, and Sen [8, 10] and later explicitly by Renner [14, Chapter 3] and Datta [2]. The metric initially used for the smoothness parameter ε\varepsilon was the trace distance. The fidelity of quantum states gives us a more natural metric in typical applications, and we adopt this measure of closeness in the article.

Let ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) and ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) be such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho)\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). We may express the ε\varepsilon-smooth relative min-entropy 𝖲∞ε(ρ∥σ){{\mathsf{S}}}^{\varepsilon}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma) as the base-22 logarithm of the value of the following optimization problem with variables ρ′∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho^{\prime}\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) and κ∈ℝ\kappa\in{\mathbb{R}}:

minimize: κ\displaystyle\quad\kappa
subject to:
ρ′\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}\quad ⪯κ​σ\displaystyle\preceq\quad\kappa\,\sigma
Tr​ρ′\displaystyle\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho^{\prime}\quad =1\displaystyle=\quad 1 (P1)
𝖥⁡(ρ,ρ′)\displaystyle{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\quad ≥1−ε\displaystyle\geq\quad 1-\varepsilon
ρ′∈L⁡(ℋ),\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}), ρ′⪰0\displaystyle\quad\rho^{\prime}\succeq 0
κ∈ℝ,\displaystyle\kappa\in{\mathbb{R}}, κ≥0\displaystyle\quad\kappa\geq 0

Here 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)=𝖽𝖾𝖿‖ρ′​ρ‖tr2{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\left\|\sqrt{\rho^{\prime}}\sqrt{\rho}\right\|_{\mathrm{tr}}^{2}, denotes the fidelity between the two quantum states, and ‖M‖tr=𝖽𝖾𝖿Tr​M†​M\left\|M\right\|_{\mathrm{tr}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\sqrt{M^{\dagger}M} denotes the trace norm of the linear operator M∈L⁡(ℋ)M\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}). The existence of a pair ρ′,κ\rho^{\prime},\kappa that are feasible for the problem (P1) means that there is a quantum state ρ′\rho^{\prime} with fidelity 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon that is also a (log2⁡κ)(\log_{2}\kappa)-substate of σ\sigma. The substate constraint implies that κ≥1\kappa\geq 1.

The program (P1) is feasible, as ρ′=𝖽𝖾𝖿ρ\rho^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\rho and κ=𝖽𝖾𝖿1/λ\kappa\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}1/\lambda, where λ\lambda is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of σ\sigma, satisfy all the constraints. Therefore we may restrict the optimization to κ∈[0,1/λ]\kappa\in[0,1/\lambda] and the compact set of quantum states with fidelity at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon with ρ\rho. The ε\varepsilon-smooth relative min-entropy between the two states is thus always achieved.

If ρ\rho is a cc-substate of σ\sigma, i.e., their relative min-entropy is at most cc, then their relative entropy 𝖲(ρ∥σ)=𝖽𝖾𝖿Trρ(log2ρ−log2σ){{\mathsf{S}}}(\rho\|\sigma)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho(\log_{2}\rho-\log_{2}\sigma) is also at most cc. Jain et al. [8, 10] gave a weak converse to this relation via the Quantum Substate Theorem, which gives a bound on the ε\varepsilon-smooth relative min-entropy in terms of the more familiar notion of relative entropy. This theorem may also be viewed as a handy operational interpretation of the rather abstract notion of relative entropy.

The substate theorem (classical or quantum) lies at the heart of a growing number of applications [10, Section 1]. These include privacy trade-offs in communication protocols for computing relations [9], message compression leading to direct sum theorems in classical and quantum communication complexity [9], impossibility results for bit-string commitment [4], the communication complexity of remote state preparation [3], and direct product theorems for classical communication complexity [6, 5]. To highlight one of these examples, the Quantum Substate Theorem enables (non-oblivious) compression of an ensemble of mixed quantum states to within a constant factor of the Holevo information of the ensemble, given access to shared entanglement and classical communication, when we are allowed a small loss of fidelity in the compression process. In contrast, the compression of arbitrary ensembles of mixed quantum states to the Holevo limit remains an open problem in quantum information theory.

Jain et al. formulated their bound in terms of a new information theoretic quantity, observational divergence 𝖣(ρ∥σ){{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma), rather than relative entropy.

Definition 1 (Observational divergence).

Let ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}). Their observational divergence is defined as

𝖣(ρ∥σ)=𝖽𝖾𝖿sup{(TrMρ)log2Tr​M​ρTr​M​σ:M∈P(ℋ),TrMσ≠0}.{{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma)\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\quad\sup\left\{(\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho)\log_{2}\frac{\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho}{\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma}\;:\;M\in{{\mathrm{P}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}),\;\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\neq 0\right\}\kern 5.0pt.

The supremum in the definition above is achieved if and only if supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho)\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). As is evident, this quantity is a scaled measure of the maximum factor by which Tr⁡(M​ρ)\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(M\rho) may exceed Tr⁡(M​σ)\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(M\sigma) for any measurement outcome MM of interest. Observational divergence is related to relative entropy. In particular, 𝖣(ρ∥σ)≤𝖲(ρ∥σ)+1{{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma)\leq{{\mathsf{S}}}(\rho\|\sigma)+1. However, it could be smaller than relative entropy by a factor proportional to the dimension [10, Proposition 4] (see also [7]).

We present alternative proofs of the Quantum Substate Theorem, also strengthening it in the process.

Theorem 1.

Let ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}} be a Hilbert space, and let ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) be quantum states such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho)\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). For any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there is a quantum state ρ′\rho^{\prime} with fidelity 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon such that ρ′⪯κ​σ\rho^{\prime}\preceq\kappa\sigma, where

κ=11−ε 2𝖣(ρ∥σ)/ε.\kappa\quad=\quad\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\;2^{{{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma)/\varepsilon}\kern 5.0pt.

Equivalently, for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1),

𝖲∞ε(ρ∥σ)≤𝖣(ρ∥σ)ε+log211−ε.{{\mathsf{S}}}^{\varepsilon}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma)\quad\leq\quad\frac{{{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma)}{\varepsilon}+\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\kern 5.0pt.

The proofs that we present are both shorter and conceptually simpler than the original proof. The proof due to Jain et al. consists of a number of technical steps, several of which are bundled into a “divergence lifting” theorem that reduces the problem to one in which ρ\rho is a pure state (a rank one quantum state). Finally, the pure state case is translated into a problem in two dimensions which is solved by a direct calculation. Divergence lifting involves going from a construction of a suitable state ρ′\rho^{\prime} for a fixed POVM element to one that is independent of the POVM element, by appealing to a minimax theorem from Game Theory. We show that this minimax theorem can be applied directly to establish the Quantum Substate Theorem. The resulting statement is stronger in its dependence on observational divergence. The original bound read as 𝖲∞ε(ρ∥σ)≤d′/ε−log2(1−ε){{\mathsf{S}}}^{\varepsilon}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma)\leq d^{\prime}/\varepsilon-\log_{2}(1-\varepsilon), where d′=𝖽𝖾𝖿d+4​d+2+2​log2⁡(d+2)+6d^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}d+4\sqrt{d+2}+2\log_{2}(d+2)+6 with d=𝖽𝖾𝖿𝖣(ρ∥σ)d\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}{{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma). The formulation in terms of fidelity also allows us to show that the dependence on observational divergence in Theorem 1 is optimal up to a constant factor.

Theorem 2.

Let ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}} be a Hilbert space, and let ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) be quantum states such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho)\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). Suppose k∈ℝk\in{\mathbb{R}} is such that for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there is a quantum state ρ′\rho^{\prime} with fidelity 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon such that ρ′⪯κ​σ\rho^{\prime}\preceq\kappa\sigma, where

κ=11−ε​ 2k/ε,\kappa\quad=\quad\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\;2^{k/\varepsilon}\kern 5.0pt,

or equivalently,

𝖲∞ε(ρ∥σ)≤kε+log211−ε.{{\mathsf{S}}}^{\varepsilon}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma)\quad\leq\quad\frac{k}{\varepsilon}+\log_{2}\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\kern 5.0pt.

Then 𝖣(ρ∥σ)≤4k+3{{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma)\leq 4k+3.

We thus settle two questions posed by Jain et al. [10, Section 5].

For the first proof (Section 2), we start by converting the convex minimization problem (P1) into a min-max problem through a simple duality argument. The minimax theorem now applies and reduces the problem of construction of a suitable state ρ′\rho^{\prime} to one that works for a fixed POVM element. The latter task turns out to be similar to proving the Classical Substate Theorem. This proof is thus shorter and conceptually simpler than the original one, and also leads to a tighter dependence on observational divergence. We present a second proof based on semi-definite programming (SDP) duality (Section 3). We believe that both approaches have their own merits. The first approach is more intuitive in that once the problem is formulated as a min-max program, the subsequent steps emerge naturally. The second approach has the appeal of relying on the more standard SDP duality. These routes to the theorem may prove useful in its burgeoning list of applications, as also in the study of smooth relative min-entropy.

2 A proof based on min-max duality

In this section, we present an alternative proof of the Quantum Substate Theorem. It hinges on a powerful minimax theorem from game theory, which is a consequence of the Kakutani fixed point theorem in real analysis [13, Propositions 20.3 and 22.2].

Theorem 3.

Let A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} be non-empty, convex and compact subsets of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} for some positive integer nn. Let u:A1×A2→ℝu:A_{1}\times A_{2}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} be a continuous function such that

  • •

    ∀a2∈A2\forall a_{2}\in A_{2}, the set {a1∈A1:(∀a1′∈A1)​u​(a1,a2)≥u⁡(a1′,a2)}\{a_{1}\in A_{1}\;:\;(\forall a_{1}^{\prime}\in A_{1})\;u(a_{1},a_{2})\geq u(a_{1}^{\prime},a_{2})\} is convex, i.e., for every a2∈A2a_{2}\in A_{2}, the set of points a1∈A1a_{1}\in A_{1} such that u⁡(a1,a2)u(a_{1},a_{2}) is maximum is a convex set; and

  • •

    ∀a1∈A1\forall a_{1}\in A_{1}, the set {a2∈A2:(∀a2′∈A2)​u​(a1,a2)≤u⁡(a1,a2′)}\{a_{2}\in A_{2}\;:\;(\forall a_{2}^{\prime}\in A_{2})\;u(a_{1},a_{2})\leq u(a_{1},a_{2}^{\prime})\} is convex, i.e., for every a1∈A1a_{1}\in A_{1}, the set of points a2∈A2a_{2}\in A_{2}, such that u⁡(a1,a2)u(a_{1},a_{2}) is minimum is a convex set.

Then, there is an (a1∗,a2∗)∈A1×A2(a_{1}^{\ast},a_{2}^{\ast})\in A_{1}\times A_{2} such that

maxa1∈A1⁡mina2∈A2⁡u⁡(a1,a2)=u⁡(a1∗,a2∗)=mina2∈A2⁡maxa1∈A1⁡u⁡(a1,a2).\max_{a_{1}\in A_{1}}\,\min_{a_{2}\in A_{2}}u(a_{1},a_{2})\quad=\quad u(a_{1}^{\ast},a_{2}^{\ast})\quad=\quad\min_{a_{2}\in A_{2}}\,\max_{a_{1}\in A_{1}}u(a_{1},a_{2})\kern 5.0pt.

We start with the following lemma which bounds the distance between a quantum state and its normalized projection onto a subspace in which it has “large” support. It is a variant of the “gentle measurement lemma” due to Winter [16].

Lemma 4.

Let ρ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) be a quantum state in the Hilbert space ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}. Let Π\Pi be an orthogonal projection onto a subspace of ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}} such that Tr​Π​ρ=δ<1\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho=\delta<1. Let ρ′′=(I−Π)​ρ​(I−Π)\rho^{\prime\prime}=({{\mathrm{I}}}-\Pi)\rho({{\mathrm{I}}}-\Pi) be the projection of ρ\rho onto the orthogonal subspace, and let ρ′=ρ′′Tr​ρ′′\rho^{\prime}=\frac{\rho^{\prime\prime}}{\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho^{\prime\prime}} be this state normalized. Then 𝖥⁡(ρ,ρ′)≥1−δ{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\geq 1-\delta.

Proof: Let 𝒦{{\mathcal{K}}} be a Hilbert space with dim(𝒦)=dim(ℋ)\dim({{\mathcal{K}}})=\dim({{\mathcal{H}}}). Let |v⟩∈𝒦⊗ℋ|v\rangle\in{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} be a purification of ρ\rho [12]. Let |v′′⟩=(I⊗(I−Π))​|v⟩|v^{\prime\prime}\rangle=({{\mathrm{I}}}\otimes({{\mathrm{I}}}-\Pi))|v\rangle. Let |v′⟩=|v′′⟩/‖v′′‖|v^{\prime}\rangle=|v^{\prime\prime}\rangle/\left\|v^{\prime\prime}\right\|. Observe that Tr𝒦​|v′′⟩​⟨v′′|=ρ′′\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}_{{{\mathcal{K}}}}\,|v^{\prime\prime}\rangle\!\langle v^{\prime\prime}|=\rho^{\prime\prime}, so

‖v′′‖2=Tr⁡|v′′⟩​⟨v′′|=Tr​ρ′′=Tr​ρ−Tr​Π​ρ=1−δ,\left\|v^{\prime\prime}\right\|^{2}\quad=\quad\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,|v^{\prime\prime}\rangle\!\langle v^{\prime\prime}|\quad=\quad\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho^{\prime\prime}\quad=\quad\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho-\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho\quad=\quad 1-\delta\kern 5.0pt,

and Tr𝒦​|v′⟩​⟨v′|=ρ′\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}_{{\mathcal{K}}}\,|v^{\prime}\rangle\!\langle v^{\prime}|=\rho^{\prime}. Now,

𝖥⁡(ρ,ρ′)\displaystyle{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\quad ≥𝖥⁡(|v⟩​⟨v|,|v′⟩​⟨v′|)\displaystyle\geq\quad{{\mathsf{F}}}(|v\rangle\!\langle v|,|v^{\prime}\rangle\!\langle v^{\prime}|)
=|⟨v|v′⟩|2\displaystyle=\quad|\langle v|v^{\prime}\rangle|^{2}
=‖v′′‖2=1−δ,\displaystyle=\quad\left\|v^{\prime\prime}\right\|^{2}\quad=\quad 1-\delta\kern 5.0pt,

where the first inequality follows from the monotonicity of fidelity under completely positive trace preserving (CPTP) operations [12]. ∎

The next lemma is an important step in the proof, and along with the minimax theorem (Theorem 3) yields the Quantum Substate Theorem. It mimics the proof of the Classical Substate Theorem with respect to a particular operator M⪰0M\succeq 0, which may be viewed as an unnormalized POVM element. Namely, we decompose MM into its diagonal basis, and imagine measuring with respect to this basis. If the observational divergence of ρ\rho with respect to σ\sigma is small, then for most of the basis elements, the probability of the outcome for ρ\rho is not too large relative to the probability for σ\sigma. Projecting ρ\rho onto the space spanned by these basis elements gives us a state ρ′\rho^{\prime}, close to ρ\rho, for which Tr​M​ρ′\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime} is correspondingly bounded, relative to Tr​M​σ\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma.

Lemma 5.

Suppose ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) are quantum states in the Hilbert space ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}} such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho)\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). Let d=𝖣(ρ∥σ)d={{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma), ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), and M⪰0M\succeq 0 be an operator on ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}. There exists a quantum state ρ′∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho^{\prime}\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) such that 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon and

(1−ε)⋅Tr​M​ρ′≤2d/ε⋅Tr​M​σ.(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\quad\leq\quad 2^{d/\varepsilon}\cdot\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\kern 5.0pt.

Proof: Consider MM in its diagonal form M=∑i=1dim(ℋ)pi​|vi⟩​⟨vi|M=\sum_{i=1}^{\dim({{\mathcal{H}}})}p_{i}|v_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i}|, where the (pi)(p_{i}) are the eigenvalues of MM corresponding to the orthonormal eigenvectors (|vi⟩)(|v_{i}\rangle). Let

B=𝖽𝖾𝖿{i:⟨vi|ρ|vi⟩>2d/ε⋅⟨vi|σ|vi⟩, 1≤i≤dim(ℋ)}.B\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\quad\left\{i\;:\;\langle v_{i}|\rho|v_{i}\rangle>2^{d/\varepsilon}\cdot\langle v_{i}|\sigma|v_{i}\rangle,\;1\leq i\leq\dim({{\mathcal{H}}})\right\}\kern 5.0pt.

Let Π=∑i∈B|vi⟩​⟨vi|\Pi=\sum_{i\in B}|v_{i}\rangle\!\langle v_{i}| be the projector onto the space spanned by vectors specified by BB. Then Tr​Π​ρ>2d/ε⋅Tr​Π​σ\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho>2^{d/\varepsilon}\cdot\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\sigma and hence,

d≥(Tr​Π​ρ)​log2​Tr​Π​ρTr​Π​σ>(Tr​Π​ρ)⋅dε.d\quad\geq\quad\left(\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho\right)\log_{2}\frac{\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho}{\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\sigma}\quad>\quad\left(\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho\right)\cdot\frac{d}{\varepsilon}\kern 5.0pt.

This implies that Tr​Π​ρ<ε\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\Pi\rho<\varepsilon. Let ρ′′=(I−Π)​ρ​(I−Π)\rho^{\prime\prime}=({{\mathrm{I}}}-\Pi)\rho({{\mathrm{I}}}-\Pi) and ρ′=ρ′′Tr​ρ′′≺ρ′′1−ε\rho^{\prime}=\frac{\rho^{\prime\prime}}{\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}{\rho^{\prime\prime}}}\prec\frac{\rho^{\prime\prime}}{1-\varepsilon}. From Lemma 4 we have 𝖥⁡(ρ,ρ′)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\geq 1-\varepsilon. Finally, by the definition of Π\Pi,

(1−ε)⋅Tr​M​ρ′\displaystyle(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\quad ≤Tr​M​ρ′′\displaystyle\leq\quad\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime\prime}
=∑i∉Bpi​⟨vi|ρ|vi⟩\displaystyle=\quad\sum_{i\not\in B}p_{i}\langle v_{i}|\rho|v_{i}\rangle
≤2d/ε​∑i∉Bpi​⟨vi|σ|vi⟩\displaystyle\leq\quad 2^{d/\varepsilon}\sum_{i\not\in B}p_{i}\langle v_{i}|\sigma|v_{i}\rangle
≤2d/ε⋅Tr​M​σ.\displaystyle\leq\quad 2^{d/\varepsilon}\cdot\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\kern 5.0pt.

∎

We now prove the main result, Theorem 1. For this, it suffices to produce a state close to ρ\rho that when scaled suitably is a substate of σ\sigma. The condition ρ′⪯κ​σ\rho^{\prime}\preceq\kappa\,\sigma is equivalent to Tr​M​ρ′≤κ\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\leq\kappa for all M⪰0M\succeq 0 with Tr​M​σ≤1\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\leq 1. We use this dual view of the substate condition to convert the minimization problem (P1) into a min-max optimization problem. We then use the minimax theorem, Theorem 3, to drastically simplify the search for a suitable state ρ′\rho^{\prime}. As a consequence, it suffices to produce a state ρ′\rho^{\prime} close to ρ\rho such that Tr​M​ρ′≤κ\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\leq\kappa for an arbitrary but fixed M⪰0M\succeq 0 with Tr​M​σ≤1\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\leq 1.

Proof of Theorem 1: We first massage the program (P1) into a form to which Theorem 3 applies. If a pair ρ′,κ\rho^{\prime},\kappa are feasible for (P1), then supp⁡(ρ′)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho^{\prime})\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). By taking ℋ=supp⁡(σ){{\mathcal{H}}}={\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma) if necessary, we may therefore assume that σ≻0\sigma\succ 0, i.e., σ\sigma has full support. It is straightforward to check that for any given ρ′∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho^{\prime}\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}),

minκ:ρ′⪯κ​σκ=maxM⪰0:Tr​M​σ≤ 1TrMρ′.\min_{\kappa~:~\rho^{\prime}\preceq\,\kappa\sigma}\kappa\quad=\quad\max_{M\succeq 0~:~\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\,\leq\,1}\;\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\kern 5.0pt.

Hence we may rewrite 𝖲∞ε(ρ∥σ){{\mathsf{S}}}^{\varepsilon}_{\infty}(\rho\|\sigma) as the base-22 logarithm of

minρ′⪰0:Tr​ρ′=1,𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥ 1−εmaxM⪰0:Tr​M​σ≤ 1TrMρ′.\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho^{\prime}\succeq 0~:~\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho^{\prime}=1,\\ {{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\,\geq\,1-\varepsilon\end{subarray}}\quad\max_{M\succeq 0~:~\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\,\leq\,1}\quad\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\kern 5.0pt.

We get

=maxM⪰ 0:Tr​M​σ≤ 1minρ′⪰ 0:Tr​ρ′= 1,𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥ 1−εTrMρ′.\displaystyle\quad=\quad\max_{M\,\succeq\,0~:~\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\sigma\,\leq\,1}\quad\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho^{\prime}\,\succeq\,0~:~\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,\rho^{\prime}\,=\,1,\\ {{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\,\geq\,1-\varepsilon\end{subarray}}\quad\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,M\rho^{\prime}\kern 5.0pt.

The desired result now follows. ∎

Combining Theorem 1 and the Uhlmann theorem [12] immediately gives us the following statement. The Quantum Substate Theorem is often used in this form in its applications.

Corollary 6.

Let ℋ,𝒦{{\mathcal{H}}},{{\mathcal{K}}} be Hilbert spaces with dim(𝒦)≥dim(ℋ)\dim({{\mathcal{K}}})\geq\dim({{\mathcal{H}}}), and let ρ,σ∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) be quantum states such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ){\mathrm{supp}}(\rho)\subseteq{\mathrm{supp}}(\sigma). Let d=𝖣(ρ∥σ)d={{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma), ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), and |v⟩∈𝒦⊗ℋ|v\rangle\in{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} be a purification of ρ\rho. Then there is a pure state |v′⟩∈𝒦⊗ℋ|v^{\prime}\rangle\in{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} with 𝖥⁡(|v⟩​⟨v|,|v′⟩​⟨v′|)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(|v\rangle\!\langle v|,|v^{\prime}\rangle\!\langle v^{\prime}|)\geq 1-\varepsilon, and a pure state |w′⟩∈𝒦⊗ℋ|w^{\prime}\rangle\in{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} such that |w⟩∈ℂ2⊗𝒦⊗ℋ|w\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\otimes{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} defined as

|w⟩=𝖽𝖾𝖿α​|0⟩​|v′⟩+1−α​|1⟩​|w′⟩,|w\rangle\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptsize{\mathsf{def}}}}{{=}}\quad\sqrt{\alpha}\;|0\rangle|v^{\prime}\rangle+\sqrt{1-\alpha}\;|1\rangle|w^{\prime}\rangle\kern 5.0pt,

with α=(1−ε)2−d/ε\alpha=(1-\varepsilon)2^{-d/\varepsilon}, is a purification of σ\sigma.

Proof: Let ρ′\rho^{\prime} be a state given by Theorem 1 such that fidelity 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon and α​ρ′⪯σ\alpha\rho^{\prime}\preceq\sigma. Then we can decompose σ\sigma as

σ=α​ρ′+(1−α)​θ,\sigma\quad=\quad\alpha\rho^{\prime}+(1-\alpha)\theta\kern 5.0pt,

where θ∈𝖣⁡(ℋ)\theta\in{{\mathsf{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) is some quantum state. By the Uhlmann theorem [12] there is a purification |v′⟩∈𝒦⊗ℋ|v^{\prime}\rangle\in{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} of ρ′\rho^{\prime} such that 𝖥⁡(|v⟩​⟨v|,|v′⟩​⟨v′|)=𝖥⁡(ρ,ρ′)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(|v\rangle\!\langle v|,|v^{\prime}\rangle\!\langle v^{\prime}|)={{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\geq 1-\varepsilon. Let |w′⟩∈𝒦⊗ℋ|w^{\prime}\rangle\in{{\mathcal{K}}}\otimes{{\mathcal{H}}} be any purification of θ\theta. Then we may verify that |w⟩|w\rangle as defined in the statement of the corollary is a purification of σ\sigma. ∎

3 A proof based on SDP duality

In this section we present a second alternative proof of the Quantum Substate Theorem, Theorem 1. The proof is based on a formulation of smooth relative min-entropy as a semi-definite program.

The optimization problem (P1) in Section 1 is seen to be an SDP once we express the fidelity constraint as a semi-definite inequality. This is based on a formulation due to Watrous [15] of the fidelity of two quantum states as an SDP. For completeness, we include a proof of its correctness.

Lemma 8 (Watrous).

Suppose ρ,ρ′∈D⁡(ℋ)\rho,\rho^{\prime}\in{{\mathrm{D}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) are quantum states in the Hilbert space ℋ{{\mathcal{H}}}. The fidelity 𝖥⁡(ρ,ρ′){{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho,\rho^{\prime}) of the two states equals the square of the optimum of the following SDP over the variable X∈L⁡(ℋ)X\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}).

maximize: 12​(Tr​X+Tr​X†)\displaystyle\quad\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,X+\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,X^{\dagger}\right)
subject to:
(ρ′XX†ρ)⪰0\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\rho^{\prime}&X\\ X^{\dagger}&\rho\end{array}\right)\quad\succeq\quad 0 (P2)\displaystyle\mathrm{(P2)}
X∈L⁡(ℋ)\displaystyle X\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}})

Proof: By Theorem IX.5.9 in the text [1], the matrix inequality in the program (P2) holds iff there is an operator Y∈L⁡(ℋ)Y\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) such that ‖Y‖≤1\left\|Y\right\|\leq 1 and X=ρ′​Y​ρX=\sqrt{\rho^{\prime}}\,Y\sqrt{\rho}. Since 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)=‖ρ′​ρ‖tr2{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)=\left\|\sqrt{\rho^{\prime}}\sqrt{\rho}\right\|_{\mathrm{tr}}^{2} and we may characterize trace norm as ‖M‖tr=max{|Tr(ZM)|:Z∈L(ℋ),‖Z‖≤1}\left\|M\right\|_{\mathrm{tr}}=\max\left\{\left|\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(ZM)\right|\;:\;Z\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}),\left\|Z\right\|\leq 1\right\} for any M∈L⁡(ℋ)M\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}), the lemma follows. ∎

The problem (P1) may now be formulated as the following SDP with variables κ∈ℝ,ρ′∈L⁡(ℋ),X∈L⁡(ℋ)\kappa\in{\mathbb{R}},\rho^{\prime}\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}),X\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) in the primal problem, and variables Z1,Z2∈L⁡(ℋ)Z_{1},Z_{2}\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) and z3,z4∈ℝz_{3},z_{4}\in{\mathbb{R}} in the dual, where Z1,Z2Z_{1},Z_{2} are Hermitian.

subject to:

The equivalence of the problems (P1) and (P3) follows from Lemma 8 and paves the way for the second proof.

Proof of Theorem 1: We may verify that strong duality holds since the P3 primal program is feasible, and the dual is strictly feasible [15, 11]. Therefore, it suffices to bound the dual objective function for any set of dual feasible variables (Z1,Z2,z3,z4)(Z_{1},Z_{2},z_{3},z_{4}).

By Lemma 5, there is a quantum state ρ′\rho^{\prime}, with 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon, such that (1−ε)​Tr​(Z1​ρ′)≤2d/ε​Tr​(Z1​σ)≤2d/ε(1-\varepsilon)\,\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(Z_{1}\rho^{\prime})\leq 2^{d/\varepsilon}\,\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(Z_{1}\sigma)\leq 2^{d/\varepsilon}, where d=𝖣(ρ∥σ)d={{\mathsf{D}}}(\rho\|\sigma).

Since 𝖥⁡(ρ′,ρ)≥1−ε{{\mathsf{F}}}(\rho^{\prime},\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon, by Lemma 8, there is an operator X∈L⁡(ℋ)X\in{{\mathrm{L}}}({{\mathcal{H}}}) such that

and Tr​X+Tr​X†≥2​1−ε\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,X+\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,X^{\dagger}\geq 2\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}. Therefore,

Tr⁡(ρ′XX†ρ)​(z4​I−Z1z3​Iz3​IZ2)≤0,\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\rho^{\prime}&X\\ X^{\dagger}&\rho\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}z_{4}{{\mathrm{I}}}-Z_{1}&z_{3}{{\mathrm{I}}}\\ z_{3}{{\mathrm{I}}}&Z_{2}\end{array}\right)\quad\leq\quad 0\kern 5.0pt,

In other words,

z4−Tr⁡(Z1​ρ′)+z3​(Tr​X+Tr​X†)+Tr⁡(Z2​ρ)\displaystyle z_{4}-\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(Z_{1}\rho^{\prime})+z_{3}(\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,X+\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}\,X^{\dagger})+\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(Z_{2}\rho) ≤\displaystyle\leq 0,\displaystyle 0\kern 5.0pt,

which implies that the dual objective function is bounded as

z4+2​z3​1−ε+Tr⁡(Z2​ρ)\displaystyle z_{4}+2z_{3}\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}+\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(Z_{2}\rho) ≤\displaystyle\leq Tr⁡(Z1​ρ′)≤2d/ε1−ε.\displaystyle\mathsf{{\mathrm{Tr}}}(Z_{1}\rho^{\prime})\quad\leq\frac{2^{d/\varepsilon}}{1-\varepsilon}\kern 5.0pt.

This completes the proof. ∎

4 Conclusion

We presented two alternative proofs of the Quantum Substate Theorem due to Jain, Radhakrishnan, and Sen [8, 10]. In addition to giving bounds on the smooth relative min-entropy of two quantum states, this gives us a powerful operational interpretation of relative entropy and observational divergence. In the process, we resolve two questions left open by Jain et al..

The crucial insight here is that the we may express smooth relative min-entropy as a convex or semi-definite program and appeal to duality theory. In this respect, we join a growing number of applications of convex and semi-definite programming to quantum information processing. This approach can be extended to the more general notion of smooth relative min-entropy studied by Renner [14] to get similar bounds on this quantity. This view of the quantity may shed light on its numerous applications.

Acknowledgements

For helpful discussions and pointers to the literature, we thank Matthias Christandl, Rajat Mittal, Marco Piani, Renato Renner, Pranab Sen, and John Watrous.

Our first attempt at this work involved an awkward formulation of smooth relative min-entropy defined with trace distance as a semi-definite program. We set aside this formulation in favour of the min-max program, which we believe also leads to a more intuitive proof. We thank John Watrous for sharing a simple SDP formulation (with a bound on trace distance) and the resulting proof. Our current presentation involving fidelity supersedes this.

Finally, we thank the referees for their extensive feedback. It lead not only to what we hope is a vastly improved presentation of the work, but also to the discovery of a tight connection between smooth relative min-entropy and observational divergence.
